title: Noise, Cognitive Function, and Worker Productivity
research_question: Do noisy workplaces impair workers' cognitive functions, does this lower earnings, and are workers aware of these effects?

participants.description: Manual laborers (128 in Exp 1, 213 in Exp 2) from Nairobi, Kenya, accustomed to factory noise and seeking employment in textile factories.
participants.recruitment: Recruited from groups of manual laborers gathering at factory gates in Nairobi, Kenya.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Engine noise from a car engine (used for automechanic training) added to ambient sewing machine noise. Control condition was ambient sewing machine noise. Noise levels were continuously monitored and did not exceed 80 dB. Treatment increased noise by ~7 dB (Exp 1) or ~9.4 dB (Exp 2), analogous to a dishwasher vs. vacuum cleaner.

measures.instrument: Number of pockets sewn, total points earned (quantity + quality), number of pockets meeting various quality criteria (1-6). Inverse hyperbolic sine transformation used for analysis.

Index (first factor of common factor analysis of percentage correct and reaction times) derived from a battery of tests measuring attention, working memory, inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, and higher-level reasoning.
Key presses on an A/B alternation task (DellaVigna and Pope 2018) over ten minutes.
Modified Becker, DeGroot, and Marschak (BDM) procedure using a binary search over KSh0-200, deducted from future earnings.
Respondents distributed 10 beans across 10 bins of possible scores for future sessions in quiet and noise under different compensation schemes.
Noise level (A-weighted decibels), CO2 (parts per million), Humidity (percent), Temperature (degrees Celsius).
Saving/withdrawal decisions, maize flour purchase decisions (inattention test), willingness to work additional hour for piece rate.

mechanisms: Noise impairs cognitive function (attention, working memory, inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, higher-level reasoning).
Workers neglect the productive impact of noise, failing to incorporate it into their willingness to pay for quiet working conditions.
Workers hold incorrect or imprecise beliefs about the impact of noise on their productivity, and are unwilling to stake money on these beliefs.
moderators: Typical noise exposure in daily life (no significant moderation)
Prompting beliefs before WTP elicitation (no significant moderation)
implementation_implications: Policymakers should consider noise pollution as a significant impediment to worker productivity in low- and middle-income countries.
Simple regulations (e.g., limiting car horn volume) could reduce noise levels without significant efficiency costs.
Governments/NGOs could raise awareness among workers and firms about the potential effects of noise on productivity to improve outcomes at minimal cost.

limitations: Logistical constraints prevented sufficiently long exposure to noise to fully assess adaptation or learning effects.
Noise levels were kept below dangerous thresholds for ethical reasons, so results may not generalize to higher, unsafe noise levels.
The production task (sewing pockets) was chosen to minimize communication, limiting generalizability to tasks requiring communication.
The sample's homogeneity in typical noise exposure may limit the ability to detect heterogeneity in effects.
The experiment was not specifically designed to test the 'inattention during production' model directly.
Workers might not have perceived the need to reduce noise further given that experimental noise levels were lower than typical factory noise.
Workers might form correct beliefs about noise effects given more time than provided in the experiment.
The study does not assess firms' awareness of noise effects, their screening practices, or abatement decisions.

paper_metadata.title: Noise, Cognitive Function, and Worker Productivity
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Noise, Cognitive Function, and Worker Productivity
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Noisy workplaces common in low- and middle-income countries can impair workers' cognitive functions. However, whether this lowers earnings depends on the importance of these functions for productivity and whether workers understand these effects. I study these questions with two randomized experiments in Nairobi, Kenya. I find a noise increase of 7 dB reduces productivity in a textile training course by 3 percent, impairs cognitive function, but does not affect effort. I also find willingness to pay for quiet working conditions does not depend on whether pay depends on performance, suggesting participants are not aware that quiet would increase their productivity. (JEL D12, J24, J28, J31, J81, O15, Q53)

environmental_features: Engine noise (various types, e.g., car engine, aircraft engine)
Specific noise levels (e.g., 50 dB, 65 dB, 80 dB)
stimulus_description.duration_exposure: 30 minutes per experimental block, within 1-hour experimental sessions

mechanism_chain.description: Environmental noise acts as a distractor, increasing cognitive load and diverting attentional resources, which subsequently impairs cognitive function and reduces worker productivity.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Environmental noise increases extraneous cognitive load, thereby impairing working memory and executive functions.
Irrelevant auditory stimuli divert attentional resources from primary tasks, leading to performance decrements.

instruments_used.name: N-back task
instruments_used.description: Computerized task requiring participants to indicate if the current stimulus matches the one presented 'n' steps back.

instruments_used.name: Stroop task
instruments_used.description: Computerized task measuring reaction time and accuracy in naming the ink color of words, especially when the word itself is a color name.

instruments_used.name: NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX)
instruments_used.description: A multi-dimensional self-report questionnaire assessing mental, physical, temporal demands, performance, effort, and frustration.

instruments_used.name: Subjective Productivity Scale
instruments_used.description: A custom-designed questionnaire asking participants to rate their perceived productivity during the experimental tasks.
